blocks.title: Core Concept: Introduction ( Principles of Inheritance and Variations)

rows: Transmission of genetic characters from parents to progeny.
The degree by which progeny differ from their parents.
The process by which characters are passed on from parents to progeny; the basis of heredity.
G.J. Mendel, the scientist who formulated the laws of inheritance through his work with pea plants.
A characteristic feature of an organism (e.g., stem height, flower color).
A variable form of a character (e.g., tall or dwarf for stem height).
Segments of DNA responsible for the appearance of characters and are passed down from parent to progeny through gametes. Mendel referred to them as "factors."
Alternate forms of a gene located at homologous sites on homologous chromosomes (e.g., dominant or recessive alleles).
The allele that produces a normal enzyme required for the transformation of a substrate.
An allele that could produce a normal, less efficient, or non-functional enzyme, or no enzyme at all.
The allele that expresses its effect even in a heterozygous state (masks the expression of the recessive allele).
The allele that only expresses its effect when two copies are present in a homozygous state (hidden in the presence of a dominant allele).
Presence of two identical alleles of a gene in a diploid organism (e.g., TT, rr).
Presence of two dissimilar alleles of a gene in a diploid organism (e.g., Tt, Rr).
The observable traits or features of an organism resulting from the genotype and the environment (e.g., tall plant, red flowers).
The genetic constitution or makeup of an organism, describing the alleles it carries (e.g., TT, Tt, or tt).
A line of organisms that, after continuous self-pollination, show stable inheritance and expression of traits for several generations.

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Mendelism ( History)
blocks.text:
Gregor Johann Mendel (1822–1884)

  • Born on 22 July 1822 at Heinzendorf in Austria at Silesia village.
  • Worked in the Augustinian Monastery as a monk in Brunn City, Austria.
  • Experimental Work: ( 1856-1863)  Seven years
  • Plant: Pisum sativum (pea plant)
  • Result Published: In 1865 / Paper name: “Experiments in Plant Hybridization”
  • Died in 1884.
After 16 years of Mendel's death in 1900, Mendel's postulates were rediscovered.

In 1900, the rediscovery of Mendel's work by three independent scientists:

  • Carl Correns
  • Hugo de Vries
  • Erich Von Tschermak
  • Use of mathematics in biology.
Reasons for Mendel's Success:

• Statistical and mathematical analysis of data.
    • Large sampling size.
    • Confirmation of his inferences from experiments on successive generations.
Mendel studied 7 characters or 7 pairs of contrasting traits in pea (Pisum sativum)

Mendel’s Experimental technique steps: ( Emasculation and Bagging Technique)

I. Selection of pure plants.
II. Hybridisation between pure plants.
(a) Emasculation    (b) Bagging
(c) Tagging            (d) Dusting
III. Selfing of F₁ hybrids to obtain F₂ generation

blocks.title: Core Conepts
blocks.text:
Monohybrid Cross: When we consider the inheritance of one character at a time in a cross this is called a monohybrid cross.
Punnett Square:
Developed by a British geneticist, Reginald C. Punnett.
The production of gametes by the parents, the formation of the zygotes, the F₁ and F₂ plants can be understood from a diagram called Punnett Square.

Since the Tt plant is heterozygous for genes controlling one character (height), it is a monohybrid and the cross between TT and tt is a monohybrid cross.

$F_{1}$ resembled either of the two parents (dominant parent)

The 1/4: 1/2: 1/4 ratio of TT: Tt: tt is mathematically condensable to the form of the binomial expression $ (ax + by)^2 $ that has the gametes bearing genes T or t in the equal frequency of 1/2

$\begin{aligned} (1 / 2 \mathrm{~T}+1 / 2 \mathrm{t})^2 & =(1 / 2 \mathrm{~T}+1 / 2 \mathrm{t}) \mathrm{X}(1 / 2 \mathrm{~T}+1 / 2 \mathrm{t}) \\ & =1 / 4 \mathrm{TT}+1 / 2 \mathrm{Tt}+1 / 4 \mathrm{tt} \end{aligned}$

LAWS BASED ON MONOHYBRID CROSS:

1. Law of dominance:

  • Characters are controlled by discrete units called factors.
  • Factors occur in pair.
  • In a dissimilar pair of factors one member of the pair dominates (dominant) the other (recessive)
  • The law of dominance is used to explain the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the $F_1 $ and the expression of both in the $F_2$.
II. Law of segregation:

This law is based on fact that the alleles do not show any blending and that both the characters are recovered as such in the $F_{2}$ generation, thought one of these is not seen at the $F_{1}$ stage.

blocks.title: Question: 2
blocks.question:
In pea plants, the allele for round seeds (R) is dominant over the allele for wrinkled seeds (r). What is the expected phenotypic ratio of offspring resulting from a cross between two heterozygous plants (Rr × Rr)?

A) 1:2:1
B) 3:1
C) 2:2
D) 1:1:1
blocks.answer:
Answer: B) 3:1

The correct answer is:
B) 3:1

Explanation:

In pea plants, the allele for round seeds (R) is dominant over the allele for wrinkled seeds (r). When two heterozygous plants (Rr × Rr) are crossed, we can predict the phenotypic ratio using a Punnett square.

Punnett Square:

Genotypic Ratio:

  • 1 RR (homozygous dominant)
  • 2 Rr (heterozygous)
  • 1 rr (homozygous recessive)
Genotypic ratio: 1:2:1

Phenotypic Ratio:

  • Round seeds (RR + Rr): 3
  • Wrinkled seeds (rr): 1
Phenotypic ratio: 3:1

Thus, the expected phenotypic ratio of offspring is 3:1.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Dihybrid Cross: A cross in which there is the study of the inheritance of two pairs of contrasting traits.

Phenotypic ratio:

Round, yellow (9) : Round, green (3)  : Wrinkled, yellow (3) : Wrinkled, green (1)

  • Genotypic ratio:
RRYY(1) : RRYy (2) : RRyy (1) : RrYY (2) : RrYy (4) : Rryy (2)  : rrYY (1)  : rrYy (2)  : rryy (1 )

LAW BASED ON DIHYBRID CROSS:
Law of independent assortment: The law states that when two pairs of traits (2 different characters) are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters".

Note: Mendel obtained new combinations in F2 generation due to independent assortment

TRIHYBRID CROSS:

A cross in which there is study of three pairs of contrasting traits.

BACK CROSS:

A back cross is a cross in which F₁ individuals are crossed with any of their parents.

Two types of cross: 1. Out Cross

2. Test Cross

1. OUT CROSS

• When F₁ (heterozygous) individual is crossed with dominant parent then it is termed out cross.

• All the progeny obtained from this cross possess dominant character. So, any analysis is not possible in F₁ generation.

2. TEST CROSS

When  $F_{1}$ or $F_{2}$ a (Heterozygous) individual is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent, then it is called a test cross.

Monohybrid test cross

Tt x tt

Phenotypic ratio = 1 : 1

Genotypic ratio = 1 : 1

Dihybrid test cross

TtRr x ttrr

Phenotypic ratio = 1:1:1:1

Genotypic ratio = 1:1:1:1

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Incomplete dominance :

  • Phenotype of F₁ does not resemble either of the two parents and is in between the two.
  • Dominant allele is not completely dominant over recessive Allele.
E.g. (i) Flower colour in snapdragon/Dog flower (Antirrhinum sp).

(ii) Size of starch grain in pea plant.

blocks.title: Question: 1
blocks.question:
In Mirabilis, red (RR) and white (rr) flowered plant produces pink (Rr) flowers. A plant with a pink flowered plant is crossed with a plant with a white flower the expected phenotypic ratio is:
(1) red: pink: white (1: 2: 1)
(2) pink: white (1: 1)
(3) red: pink (1:1)
(4) red: white (3:1)
blocks.answer:
Ans: (2)

In Mirabilis (also known as the four o'clock plant), the inheritance of flower color follows incomplete dominance, meaning that neither allele is completely dominant over the other. The following applies:

  • Red flower (RR)
  • White flower (rr)
  • Pink flower (Rr) — a heterozygous mixture of red and white, leading to the intermediate pink color.
Now, if a pink flower (Rr) is crossed with a white flower (rr), the possible genotypes of the offspring can be determined using a Punnett square:

  • The offspring will have a 1:1 ratio of pink (Rr) and white (rr) flowers.
Thus, the expected phenotypic ratio is 1:1 (pink: white).

Therefore, the correct answer is (2) pink: white (1: 1).

The resulting genotypic ratio in the F2 generation will be:

Therefore, 25% of the offspring would have red flowers (RR).

blocks.title: Question:1
blocks.question:
A gene showing codominance has:
(1) both alleles independently expressed in the heterozygote
(2) one allele dominant on the other
(3) alleles tightly linked on the same chromosome
(4) alleles that are recessive to each other
blocks.answer:
Ans: (1)

Codominance occurs when both alleles of a gene are fully and independently expressed in the heterozygote. This is different from incomplete dominance, where the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype, and from dominance, where one allele masks the expression of the other.

In codominance:

  • Both alleles contribute equally to the phenotype.
  • For example, in the case of human blood types, the A and B alleles are codominant, so an individual with both A and B alleles (AB) will express both A and B antigens on the surface of red blood cells.
Thus, the correct statement is that both alleles are independently expressed in the heterozygote.
options: (1) both alleles independently expressed in the heterozygote

blocks.title: Core Concept: Multiple alleles
blocks.text:
Multiple alleles :

  • More than 2 alternative forms of the same gene are called multiple alleles.
  • Multiple alleles are formed due to mutation
  • If n is the number of alleles of a gene then number of different possible genotype = n (n+1) / 2.
  • More than two alternative forms of same gene are called multiple alleles e.g. ABO blood group.
  • Eg. ABO blood group are controlled by gene-I
  • The gene-I has 3 alleles:Iᴬ , Iᴮ and i
  • The alleles I and Iᴮ produce a slightly different form of the B sugar while allele i does not produce any sugar.
  • Because humans are diploid organisms, each person possesses any two of the three I gene alleles.
  • Multiple alleles and dominance

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Pleiotropy :

The gene which controls more than one character is called a pleiotropic gene.

This gene shows multiple phenotypic effects. The phenomenon is known as Pleiotropy.

Eg.,

  • Phenylketonuria
  • Starch grain size in pea
  • Single pleiotropic genes can exhibit multiple phenotypic expressions.
  • The mechanism of pleiotropy, in most cases, is the effect of a gene on metabolic pathways, which contribute towards different phenotypes.
Occasionally, a single gene product may produce more than one effect (pleiotropism)
e.g., Starch synthesis in pea seeds is controlled by one gene.
      • It has two alleles (B and b) which also controls seed shape.
      • Alleles B & b shows different levels of dominance for starch grain size and seed shape.
Therefore, dominance is not an autonomous feature of a gene or the product that it has information for.
It depends as much on the gene product and the production of a particular phenotype from this product as it does on the particular phenotype that we choose to examine, in case more than one phenotype is influenced by the same gene.

Sickel cell Anaemia :

• Gene Hbˢ β provides a classic example of pleiotropy.
    • It not only causes haemolytic anaemia but also results in increased resistance to one type of malaria that is caused by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum.
    • The sickle cell Hbˢ β allele also has a pleiotropic effect on the development of many tissues and organs such as bone, lungs, kidney, spleen, and heart.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Pleiotropy often involves multiple, seemingly unrelated traits.
  • The sickle cell trait (heterozygosity for the mutation) reduces the severity and frequency of malaria but does not grant complete immunity.
  • Plasmodium falciparum, the malaria-causing parasite, still infects these individuals, but the progression is often less severe.
  • Homozygous individuals (with two copies of the mutation) experience severe sickle cell disease, while heterozygous individuals generally have mild or no symptoms.

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance
blocks.text:
Chromosomal theory of inheritance :

1902 - chromosome (coloured bodies, as visualised by staining) movement during meiosis had been worked out.

Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri: noted that the behaviour of chromosomes was parallel to the behaviour of genes.

Metaphase of meiosis I, two chromosome pairs can align at the metaphase plate independently of each other.

Sutton United the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance.

Experimental verification Thomas Hunt Morgan and his colleagues. Morgan worked on tiny fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster:
    • grown on - simple synthetic medium

  • life cycle - about two weeks
  • single mating - large number of progeny.
  • male and female - easily distinguishable
  • many hereditary variations - seen with low power microscopes

blocks.title: Linkage and Recombination
blocks.text:
Morgan performed dihybrid crosses in Drosophila to study genes that were sex-linked.

Two genes did not segregate independently of each other. The F2 ratio deviated very significantly from the 9:3:3:1 ratio (expected when the two genes are independent).

Morgan coined linkage = physical association of genes on chromosome & recombination = non-parental gene combinations.

  • Very tightly linked genes: Showed very low recombination.
  • Loosely linked genes: Showed higher recombination.
$\text{Strength of Linkage} \propto \frac{1}{\text{crossing over (recombination)}} \propto \frac{1}{\text{distance between linked genes}}$

His student Alfred Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination (1% Recombination = 1 CentiMorgan or 1 Map Unit distance) between linked genes and 'mapped' their position on the chromosome.

Today, genetic maps are extensively used as a starting point in the sequencing of whole genomes, as was done in the case of the Human Genome Sequencing Project.

blocks.title: Question:  4
blocks.question:
In a cross between individuals homozygous for (a, b) and AaBb, 700 out of 1000 individuals were of parental type. Then the distance between a and b is :-

(1) 70 map unit (2) 35 map unit

(3) 30 map unit (4) 15 map unit
blocks.answer:
Ans- 3

Explanation:

In genetics, the distance between two genes is often measured in map units (also called centimorgans, cM). The number of map units corresponds to the frequency of recombination events between the genes during meiosis. This is calculated using the recombination frequency.

Recombination frequency = Number of recombinant offspringTotal number of offspring×100\frac{\text{Number of recombinant offspring}}{\text{Total number of offspring}} \times 100Total number of offspringNumber of recombinant offspring​×100

Step-by-step calculation:

  • Parental type: Out of 1000 offspring, 700 were of the parental type, which means they are not recombinant.
  • Recombinant offspring:
Number of recombinant offspring = Total offspring - Parental offspring
1000−700=3001000 - 700 = 3001000−700=300
  • Recombination frequency:
Recombination frequency = 3001000×100=30%\frac{300}{1000} \times 100 = 30\%1000300​×100=30%
  • Distance between genes:
The recombination frequency (30%) is equal to the map distance between the genes in centimorgans (cM). In this case, the distance between the genes a and b is 30 map units.
Thus, the distance between genes a and b is 30 map units.

blocks.title: Core Concept : Mutation
blocks.text:
Mutation :

Mutation is a phenomenon which results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently results in changes in the genotype and the phenotype of an organism.

  • In addition to recombination, mutation is another phenomenon that leads to variation in DNA.
  • Mutation arises due to:
(i) Loss (deletions) or gain (insertion/duplication) of a segment of DNA

(Frame shift Mutation)

(ii) Due to change in a single base pair of DNA ( Point Mutation) eg. Sickle cell Anaemia.

  • Chromosomal aberrations are commonly observed in cancer cells.
  • Mutagens are many chemical and physical factors that induce mutations. Eg UV radiations.

blocks.title: Common Mistake
blocks.text:
• Assuming silent mutations (which do not change the amino acid sequence) have no functional impact.
  • Using "mutation" and "polymorphism" interchangeably.
  • Failing to recognize how a frameshift mutation alters the entire downstream protein sequence.
  • Not differentiating between somatic mutations (occur in body cells and aren't heritable) and germline mutations (occur in reproductive cells and can be passed to offspring).

blocks.answer:

Sickle cell anemia is caused by a mutation in the gene that codes for the beta chain of hemoglobin. In this genetic disorder, a mutation in the HBB gene leads to the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta chain of hemoglobin. This change causes hemoglobin molecules to stick together, forming long, rigid structures that distort the shape of red blood cells into a sickle shape.

blocks.title: Question: 2
blocks.question:
Given below is a pedigree chart of a family with five children. It shows the inheritance of attached ear–lobes as opposed to the free ones. The squares represent the male individuals and circles the female individuals. Which one of the following conclusions drawn is correct :–

(1) The parents are homozygous recessive

(2) The trait is Y–linked

(3) The parents are homozygous dominant

(4) The parents are heterozygous
blocks.answer:
Ans- 4

To solve this, let's analyze the pedigree chart and the genetic trait shown:

  • Attached ear-lobe is shown by filled symbols (● or ■).
  • Free ear-lobe is shown by open symbols (○ or □).
  • Square = Male
  • Circle = Female
  • From the pedigree:
  • Both parents (top row) have free ear-lobes (open circle and open square).
  • • Some of their children have attached ear-lobes (filled symbols), and some have free ear-lobes.
Step-by-step genetic reasoning:

Let’s denote:

  • A = allele for free ear-lobe (dominant)
  • a = allele for attached ear-lobe (recessive)
If attached ear-lobe is recessive (aa), and both parents have free ear-lobes but produce children with attached ones, then:

  • Parents must carry the recessive allele (i.e., they are heterozygous Aa).
  • That’s the only way they can produce an aa (attached) child.
Conclusion:

Correct answer: (4) The parents are heterozygous

Because:

  • They have the dominant phenotype (free ear-lobe), but
  • They produce children with the recessive phenotype (attached ear-lobe), which is only possible if both parents are heterozygous (Aa).

Study the pedigree given below and assign  the type of inheritance of the trait :-

(1) X-linked recessive

(2) Y-linked

(3) autosomal recessive

(4) autosomal dominant
blocks.answer:
Ans- 3

To determine the type of inheritance from the given pedigree, let's analyze the pattern of affected individuals:

Observations:

  • Affected individuals are both male and female.
  • The trait skips generations (seen in grandparents and grandchildren but not the parents).
  • Unaffected parents have affected children (e.g., second-generation parents have third-generation affected children).
  • Equal number of affected males and females, which rules out sex-linked traits like X-linked or Y-linked inheritance.
Analysis of Options:

  • X-linked recessive – Unlikely: Affected females would need affected fathers, which isn't always the case here. Also, we'd expect more affected males than females.
  • Y-linked –  Impossible: Affected females are present. Y-linked traits only affect males.
  • Autosomal recessive –  Fits: Trait skips generations, affects both sexes equally, and affected individuals are born to unaffected carrier parents.
  • Autosomal dominant –  Would appear in every generation, not skipping any.

blocks.title: Core Concepts: Mendelism ( History)
blocks.text:
Gregor Johann Mendel (1822–1884)

  • Born on 22 July 1822 at Heinzendorf in Austria at Silesia village.
  • Worked in the Augustinian Monastery as a monk in Brunn City, Austria.
  • Experimental Work: ( 1856-1863)  Seven years
  • Plant: Pisum sativum (pea plant)
  • Result Published: In 1865 / Paper name: “Experiments in Plant Hybridization”
  • Died in 1884.
After 16 years of Mendel's death in 1900, Mendel's postulates were rediscovered.

In 1900, the rediscovery of Mendel's work by three independent scientists:

  • Carl Correns
  • Hugo de Vries
  • Erich Von Tschermak
  • Use of mathematics in biology.
Reasons for Mendel's Success:

• Statistical and mathematical analysis of data.
    • Large sampling size.
    • Confirmation of his inferences from experiments on successive generations.
Mendel studied 7 characters or 7 pairs of contrasting traits in pea (Pisum sativum)

Mendel’s Experimental technique steps: ( Emasculation and Bagging Technique)

I. Selection of pure plants.
II. Hybridisation between pure plants.
(a) Emasculation    (b) Bagging
(c) Tagging            (d) Dusting
III. Selfing of F₁ hybrids to obtain F₂ generation

blocks.title: Core Conepts
blocks.text:
Monohybrid Cross: When we consider the inheritance of one character at a time in a cross this is called a monohybrid cross.
Punnett Square:
Developed by a British geneticist, Reginald C. Punnett.
The production of gametes by the parents, the formation of the zygotes, the F₁ and F₂ plants can be understood from a diagram called Punnett Square.

Since the Tt plant is heterozygous for genes controlling one character (height), it is a monohybrid and the cross between TT and tt is a monohybrid cross.

$F_{1}$ resembled either of the two parents (dominant parent)

The 1/4: 1/2: 1/4 ratio of TT: Tt: tt is mathematically condensable to the form of the binomial expression $ (ax + by)^2 $ that has the gametes bearing genes T or t in the equal frequency of 1/2

$\begin{aligned} (1 / 2 \mathrm{~T}+1 / 2 \mathrm{t})^2 & =(1 / 2 \mathrm{~T}+1 / 2 \mathrm{t}) \mathrm{X}(1 / 2 \mathrm{~T}+1 / 2 \mathrm{t}) \\ & =1 / 4 \mathrm{TT}+1 / 2 \mathrm{Tt}+1 / 4 \mathrm{tt} \end{aligned}$

LAWS BASED ON MONOHYBRID CROSS:

1. Law of dominance:

  • Characters are controlled by discrete units called factors.
  • Factors occur in pair.
  • In a dissimilar pair of factors one member of the pair dominates (dominant) the other (recessive)
  • The law of dominance is used to explain the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the $F_1 $ and the expression of both in the $F_2$.
II. Law of segregation:

This law is based on fact that the alleles do not show any blending and that both the characters are recovered as such in the $F_{2}$ generation, thought one of these is not seen at the $F_{1}$ stage.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Dihybrid Cross: A cross in which there is the study of the inheritance of two pairs of contrasting traits.

Phenotypic ratio:

Round, yellow (9) : Round, green (3)  : Wrinkled, yellow (3) : Wrinkled, green (1)

  • Genotypic ratio:
RRYY(1) : RRYy (2) : RRyy (1) : RrYY (2) : RrYy (4) : Rryy (2)  : rrYY (1)  : rrYy (2)  : rryy (1 )

LAW BASED ON DIHYBRID CROSS:
Law of independent assortment: The law states that when two pairs of traits (2 different characters) are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters".

Note: Mendel obtained new combinations in F2 generation due to independent assortment

TRIHYBRID CROSS:

A cross in which there is study of three pairs of contrasting traits.

BACK CROSS:

A back cross is a cross in which F₁ individuals are crossed with any of their parents.

Two types of cross: 1. Out Cross

2. Test Cross

1. OUT CROSS

• When F₁ (heterozygous) individual is crossed with dominant parent then it is termed out cross.

• All the progeny obtained from this cross possess dominant character. So, any analysis is not possible in F₁ generation.

2. TEST CROSS

When  $F_{1}$ or $F_{2}$ a (Heterozygous) individual is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent, then it is called a test cross.

Monohybrid test cross

Tt x tt

Phenotypic ratio = 1 : 1

Genotypic ratio = 1 : 1

Dihybrid test cross

TtRr x ttrr

Phenotypic ratio = 1:1:1:1

Genotypic ratio = 1:1:1:1

Incomplete dominance :

In this phenomenon, both the allele of a gene expresses a particular character in F₁ progeny. There is no blending of characters, whereas both characters are expressed equally.

  • The sickle cell trait (heterozygosity for the mutation) reduces the severity and frequency of malaria but does not grant complete immunity.
  • Plasmodium falciparum, the malaria-causing parasite, still infects these individuals, but the progression is often less severe.
  • Homozygous individuals (with two copies of the mutation) experience severe sickle cell disease, while heterozygous individuals generally have mild or no symptoms.

blocks.title: Common Mistake
blocks.text:
• Assuming silent mutations (which do not change the amino acid sequence) have no functional impact.
  • Using "mutation" and "polymorphism" interchangeably.
  • Failing to recognize how a frameshift mutation alters the entire downstream protein sequence.
  • Not differentiating between somatic mutations (occur in body cells and aren't heritable) and germline mutations (occur in reproductive cells and can be passed to offspring).

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Pleiotropy :

The gene which controls more than one character is called a pleiotropic gene.

This gene shows multiple phenotypic effects. The phenomenon is known as Pleiotropy.

Eg.,

  • Phenylketonuria
  • Starch grain size in pea
  • Single pleiotropic genes can exhibit multiple phenotypic expressions.
  • The mechanism of pleiotropy, in most cases, is the effect of a gene on metabolic pathways, which contribute towards different phenotypes.
Occasionally, a single gene product may produce more than one effect (pleiotropism)
e.g., Starch synthesis in pea seeds is controlled by one gene.
      • It has two alleles (B and b) which also controls seed shape.
      • Alleles B & b shows different levels of dominance for starch grain size and seed shape.
Therefore, dominance is not an autonomous feature of a gene or the product that it has information for.
It depends as much on the gene product and the production of a particular phenotype from this product as it does on the particular phenotype that we choose to examine, in case more than one phenotype is influenced by the same gene.

Sickel cell Anaemia :

• Gene Hbˢ β provides a classic example of pleiotropy.
    • It not only causes haemolytic anaemia but also results in increased resistance to one type of malaria that is caused by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum.
    • The sickle cell Hbˢ β allele also has a pleiotropic effect on the development of many tissues and organs such as bone, lungs, kidney, spleen, and heart.

blocks.title: Core Concept: Introduction ( Principles of Inheritance and Variations)

rows: Transmission of genetic characters from parents to progeny.
The degree by which progeny differ from their parents.
The process by which characters are passed on from parents to progeny; the basis of heredity.
G.J. Mendel, the scientist who formulated the laws of inheritance through his work with pea plants.
A characteristic feature of an organism (e.g., stem height, flower color).
A variable form of a character (e.g., tall or dwarf for stem height).
Segments of DNA responsible for the appearance of characters and are passed down from parent to progeny through gametes. Mendel referred to them as "factors."
Alternate forms of a gene located at homologous sites on homologous chromosomes (e.g., dominant or recessive alleles).
The allele that produces a normal enzyme required for the transformation of a substrate.
An allele that could produce a normal, less efficient, or non-functional enzyme, or no enzyme at all.
The allele that expresses its effect even in a heterozygous state (masks the expression of the recessive allele).
The allele that only expresses its effect when two copies are present in a homozygous state (hidden in the presence of a dominant allele).
Presence of two identical alleles of a gene in a diploid organism (e.g., TT, rr).
Presence of two dissimilar alleles of a gene in a diploid organism (e.g., Tt, Rr).
The observable traits or features of an organism resulting from the genotype and the environment (e.g., tall plant, red flowers).
The genetic constitution or makeup of an organism, describing the alleles it carries (e.g., TT, Tt, or tt).
A line of organisms that, after continuous self-pollination, show stable inheritance and expression of traits for several generations.
